title: Goodnight Stories | The Empire of Roses
subtitle: Guess whom I have loved, and who has loved me?
body:
## A Word from the Author
I’m someone who starts stories and never finishes them. Just read for fun, and please don’t ask what happens next, because I don’t know either ヾ(•ω•`)o

## I

“If desire had a shape, it would surely be round. Like a snowball on a winter hillside, growing larger and larger as you roll it in your hands. You cannot stop, and must not stop; to stop is only to be crushed. And the ever-growing snowball rolling onward will blind the person pushing it, so she can no longer see any of the tragic people and fates ahead.”

The wars never ceased. Whenever a dispatch brought news of a great victory or a crushing defeat, the queen always remembered that winter, that desolate garden, and that figure who looked so thin yet stood so straight. Back then, she had only been the least-favored princess in the palace. She had few friends, and usually read alone, practiced calligraphy alone, and trained in martial arts alone. Only A-Bei occasionally kept her company and talked with her.

A-Bei was her guard and her study companion. Rumor had it that she was the king’s illegitimate child. Her mother had died in childbirth, and without her mother’s protection, A-Bei was secretly sent to the great general, where she was carelessly brought up as one of his children by a concubine. A-Bei did not care about her origins, and seemed not to care about her prospects either. Unless the princess spoke to her first, she could go an entire week without saying a word. That day, the princess had spent the afternoon reading Greek myths. She loved the stories so much that she could not resist deliberately reading aloud, secretly hoping A-Bei could hear her from nearby.

After she finished the story of Sisyphus and fell into thought, she heard a voice, gentle yet with a trace of coldness, say slowly: “If desire had a shape, it would surely be round. Like a snowball on a winter hillside, growing larger and larger as you roll it in your hands. You cannot stop, and must not stop; to stop is only to be crushed. And the ever-growing snowball rolling onward will blind the person pushing it, so she can no longer see any of the tragic people and fates ahead.”

The princess was a little surprised. The usually taciturn girl had suddenly become talkative today. She looked up at A-Bei. “If it were me, I would never choose the fate of pushing a snowball to begin with.”

A-Bei shook her head. “But often, fate is not something you choose. It is not a gift, but a compulsion.”

“If that day really came, I would rather choose to stop. Even if I were crushed, I would not want to be blinded, to hurt the innocent, or to betray my own heart.”

“But sometimes you are not the only one behind the snowball. When you look back and see so many comrades who have shared your days and nights, could you bear to sacrifice all their lives with one decision of yours?”

“That really is a difficult question! But where would I get so many comrades behind me? As I see it, there would only be you at most. A-Bei, tell me—if the day came when I truly let go, would you still stay beside me?”

“A-Bei will always stay beside the princess, as you wish.”

Ha. Always stay beside the princess. A-Bei, you liar!

The queen did not like recalling the day of the uprising: the whole palace in chaos, the glow of blood and fire reflecting one another. So military coups were not merely stories in books. Of all of them, she alone had escaped that revolt.

Sometimes she felt sad. Although her father and sisters had never cared much for her, the destruction of an entire family still brought a moment’s grief.

More often, of course, she remembered A-Bei with far more complicated feelings.

It turned out that A-Bei was not merely her father’s illegitimate child. Her birth mother had been the neighboring king’s sister. This marriage, which might have been as happy as a fairy tale, had eventually become an unspeakable palace scandal. Perhaps because it began with the scandal of her mother running away from home; perhaps because the king already had a queen and had never intended to marry her formally; perhaps because it ended in a death during childbirth whose cause remained unclear. When had A-Bei, at the center of the storm, learned of her ridiculous origins? What had she felt on confronting such a melodramatic plot, before finally choosing her mother’s side? Shanshan did not know.

All the stories, mixed with rumors, brought only one truth: General Bei had rebelled, and the Empire of Roses had fallen.

The day before Shanshan escaped the palace, A-Bei had acted out of character and brought her a bouquet of sunflowers. Sunflowers were Shanshan’s favorite flowers, because they always turned toward the light, even when they themselves were trapped in darkness. Shanshan stroked the golden petals carefully.

“A-Bei, what flowers do you like?”

“Me? I like lilies. Pure, untouched by any dust.”

“Then what flower do you think I resemble?”

“You? A rose, perhaps. Though it blooms so ardently, if someone insists on holding it in their hand, its thorns will wound them.”

She had not understood the sadness that flashed through A-Bei’s eyes then.

Nor had she foreseen that the gifts of fate were secretly marked with prices.

## II

“If you grant me thorns, my armor stays with me; if you grant me a white dove, my heart stays open.”

With what feelings did I go to see my father’s former subordinates? With what feelings did I lead the army to restore the empire? I remember none of it.

I remember only that the sunflowers on my desk no longer bloomed so ardently. I understood that it was not their fault. Humans cannot master their own fate, let alone a plant.

On the day the sunflower’s last petal fell, I gave the order to attack the imperial capital.

Recover the lost territory, reclaim the lands that had belonged to our empire—and reclaim my so-called true heart, which I had given away.

Through those days of war, I grew quickly. From an idiot princess who could barely read a campaign map, I became a wise queen who could make decisive judgments of battle and death.

Every day I received much news, about the war and about the people. But I always found myself looking for news of her.

I heard she had rendered great service and was exceptionally appointed Grand General Who Guards the Realm.

I heard she had raised the subject of a truce at the king’s victory banquet, which ended unhappily.

I heard she had been placed under house arrest. Suspicion is never lessened by blood ties; it only grows heavier with achievement.

My army advanced like split bamboo. We had recovered most of our former territory when a peace proposal finally came from the other side.

Of course, it was not only a peace proposal, but a marriage proposal too.

Her brother wanted to marry me and make me queen.

Holding that pure white proposal, that symbol of love, I laughed until tears ran down my face.

I did not know whether she knew.

If she knew, would she be sad?

If she did not, would she be surprised when we met again?

Everyone thought I would refuse. One cannot share the sky with one’s father’s murderer.

But I agreed.

It was very cold on my wedding day. In the bitter wind, I insisted on wearing white.

Before leaving the palace gates, I shaped a little snowball. It quickly changed from soft white to hard transparency. I held it for a long time, until a needle-like pain came from my left hand. So cold that penetrates the marrow was not rhetoric, but realism.

On the wedding day, I did not see her after all.

Disappointed?

It seemed not.

Because I knew a day would always come when we met again.

And that day was near.

“Henry I was murdered on his wedding day. The bride was arrested at the scene.

Henry I left no heirs. His younger sister A-Bei succeeded him, known to the world as Empress Bei.”

Ha. So vast and turbulent a story, once turned into words and placed in a history book, amounted to only two lines.

She let me go.

I asked the figure in black who released me whether there was a message to pass on.

The figure shook their head, then took from their robes a rose just about to bloom.

My tears struck its petals, making them tremble ceaselessly, like a beating heart.

You always said I was a rose, yet I never noticed my own sharpness.

Until my thorns pierced deep into your heart.
